opus-5.5.text:
I think it cuts both ways, and which way it cuts depends a lot on the details.

The optimistic case is that coordination pressure gives labs cover. Many alignment changes are things a lab might want to do but feels it can't afford to do alone: slowing a deployment to run more evaluations, holding a capability back until you understand it better, spending a larger fraction of compute on safety research rather than the next training run. If the competitive pressure is "if we don't ship, someone less careful will," then a credible government-backed floor helps. Everyone has to meet a certain bar, so meeting that bar no longer costs you relative to your competitors. That's the main way I'd hope coordination helps.

The worry is about rigidity and timing. Alignment is still a very immature field. We don't know what the right techniques are, and I expect our view of what "safe enough" means to change quite a lot over the next few years. If government coordination locks in particular procedures, such as a specific evaluation suite, a specific reporting format, or a specific definition of what counts as a dangerous capability, you risk freezing today's best guess. Then if a lab realizes, "Actually, this approach to oversight is flawed, and we need to restructure how we train these models," that change might be harder to make, not easier. It might have to go back through some approval process, or it might not count toward compliance, so there's less incentive to do it.

There's also a subtler issue. When coordination is framed mainly around national competitiveness, the pressure can run in the opposite direction from safety. If the message from government is "you're a strategic asset and you need to stay ahead," that can make it harder for a lab to say, "We're going to pause this line of work because we don't understand it." So the content of the coordination matters a lot. Coordinating on safety floors and information sharing is quite different from coordinating on racing.

So my rough view is that the most useful kind of coordination sets outcome-oriented requirements rather than prescribing methods. Something like: you need to be able to make a convincing case that this system is safe for this deployment. It should leave room for that case to be built in new ways as the science improves. It should also have mechanisms to update quickly, because the field is going to move faster than typical regulatory cycles. And ideally, it creates channels for labs to share what they're learning about failures, so that the coordination is also coordination on knowledge, not just on rules.

r001.rationale: The response says competition can discourage slowing deployment or holding back capabilities, but does not clearly state that intense competition makes it difficult to change labs’ technical approach for alignment.

r002.rationale: The response explains that government coordination can enable alignment changes through shared safety floors or hinder them by locking in procedures and making new approaches harder to adopt.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where my views have shifted a bit over the last few years. The basic picture I have is that alignment, at least the way I think about it, isn't going to be a one-shot thing where you figure out the technique and then you're done. It's much more likely to be iterative: you build a system, you find it does something slightly wrong, you go back and change how you train it, you change the reward signal, you change the oversight scheme, and you keep doing that. And that only works if the labs actually have the freedom to make those changes when they need to.

So the question becomes: what happens when there's a lot of external pressure, including from governments, pushing in a particular direction? I think there are two failure modes here, and they pull in opposite ways.

The first is the one people usually worry about, which is a race dynamic. If governments are saying, "we need capabilities, we need to stay ahead of some other country," then the pressure is to ship, and the safety work gets deprioritised. That's bad in the obvious way: you don't get to do the iteration because you don't have time.

The second one is more subtle, and I think people underweight it. It's that coordination mechanisms themselves can become rigid. If you have a regulatory framework that says "you must do X, Y, and Z before deployment," and X, Y, and Z were the best ideas we had in, say, 2024, then you've frozen the state of the art at that moment. And if it turns out that the actual thing you need to do for alignment is some technique nobody had thought of yet, the lab might have a hard time doing it, because the compliance machinery is built around the old requirements. You end up optimising for the checklist rather than for the models actually being safe.

Now, I don't want to come across as anti-regulation here. I actually think we need quite a lot of government involvement, because the labs on their own don't have the right incentives, and the stakes are too high to just hope that everyone behaves well. But the design matters enormously. The versions I'm most optimistic about are ones that regulate outcomes and evidence rather than specific techniques. So something like: you have to show that your model clears some bar on dangerous capabilities evaluations, and you have to have a credible story for how you'd catch it if the model were doing something you didn't want. That leaves the lab free to change the underlying method as understanding improves, while still giving the government a real lever.

The other thing I'd say is that the coordination pressure cuts both ways from the lab's perspective. Inside a lab, there's always a tension between the people who want to move fast and the people who want to be careful. External pressure that says "you must be careful, and here's how we'll check" can actually strengthen the hand of the careful people internally. I've seen versions of that. Someone can go into a meeting and say, "look, we can't do this because we'd fail the eval," and that's a much easier argument to win than "we shouldn't do this because I have a bad feeling about it."

So my overall take is: the pressure is probably net positive if it's done well, net negative if it's done badly, and the single most important design question is whether it preserves the ability to change your mind about what the right technique is. Because I'm pretty confident we don't have the final answer yet, and any system that assumes we do is going to be a problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says government pressure to stay ahead of another country can prioritize shipping and leave too little time for alignment iteration. It does not clearly state that competition among AI labs makes technical changes difficult.

r002.rationale: The candidate explains that government coordination and regulation can affect labs’ freedom to change alignment methods, but it does not say that even modest coordination pressure could determine that ability.

astra-6.text:
I think it could go either way. One thing you’d like government coordination to do is give labs room to make changes that would otherwise be commercially very difficult. If a lab thinks, “We need to slow down, or change our training process, or spend substantially more resources checking whether this system is safe,” it helps enormously if they know their competitors face similar requirements. Otherwise there’s pressure to keep going even when the people involved would prefer to be more cautious.

But you don’t want coordination to freeze a particular approach to alignment. We’re still learning what the problems are and what interventions actually work. If changing your approach requires renegotiating a detailed agreement among several labs and governments, that could make it harder to respond to new evidence.

So I’d want coordination around the obligation to demonstrate safety, with flexibility about how you get there. The important question is whether the pressure gives people the ability to make difficult changes when they discover a problem, or makes those changes harder.

r001.rationale: The response says competitive pressure can make changes commercially difficult and that labs may otherwise feel pressure to keep going, even when they want to change training or spend more on safety checks.

r002.rationale: The response says coordination pressure can help or hinder labs’ ability to make changes, but it does not communicate that even modest pressure could determine whether they can make those changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could go in either direction. One difficulty for a lab is that a change that makes alignment easier might also slow down development. If you’re worried that another lab will push ahead, it’s harder to make that change, even if everyone would prefer a world where all the labs made it.

Government coordination could help by making those constraints apply to everyone. Then a lab can spend more time on safety without feeling that it’s unilaterally giving up its position.

But you can also get pressure in the opposite direction. If governments frame AI as a race that they absolutely have to win, that can make it harder for the people inside labs to say, “We need to stop and rethink this.” So the important question is what governments are coordinating around: whether they’re creating room to make the changes alignment requires, or adding another reason to move faster.

r001.rationale: The response says that if a lab fears another will advance, it is harder to make a change that could slow development, even when labs would prefer that change collectively.

r002.rationale: It describes government coordination as potentially helping or hindering alignment changes, but does not state that even modest coordination pressure could determine whether labs can make them.
